| [THEORY-058](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-058.md) v2 | Mental disorders are maintained by self-reinforcing causal loops rather than expressing a latent common cause, which is how they can outlast their triggers | Three traditions that do not cite one another for it put self-sustaining loops where a latent cause would be. Borsboom ([LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md)) makes disorder an alternative stable state of a strongly connected symptom network, kept up by hysteresis after its trigger has gone. Salkovskis, Sighvatsson and Sigurdsson ([LIT-538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-538.md)) make it a threat meaning protected by the behaviour it drives. Kendler ([LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md)) finds causal loops across levels, from genes to culture. The convergence is real; the evidence is indirect, simulated or clinical, and none of it is an individual time series showing hysteresis, so the account is Proposed. It says nothing about what starts a disorder. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-097](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-097.md) | Long-range coordination in the human forebrain is carried by brief ripples that co-occur at distant sites: during them neurons co-fire more whatever the distance between them, and at retrieval they carry stimulus-specific reinstatement of encoding co-firing | Verzhbinsky, Daume, Cheng, Rutishauser & Halgren (2026), [LIT-633](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-633.md): in 1,373 single units from five bilateral forebrain regions of 35 epilepsy patients doing a Sternberg task, ripples (70–100 Hz, about 70 ms) co-occur between bundles at a median 5% at every tract distance from 71 to 223 mm, and unit pairs co-fire a median 34% more during co-ripples than in no-ripple periods, beyond a rate-only null and with no loss over distance. The gain rises with load (13% in maintenance, 19% at retrieval), and encoding co-firing for a stimulus recurs at retrieval in 0.29% of cell-pair trials in co-ripples against 0.14% outside them. Correlational throughout: one task, two load levels, clinically placed electrodes, nothing perturbed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-143](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-143.md) v2 | When a group learns only about the options its members pursue and good evidence is scarce, sparser communication makes it more likely to settle on the better option, at a large cost in speed; when evidence is plentiful, sparsity only slows learning | Zollman (2007), [LIT-724](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-724.md), simulated Bala and Goyal's bandit model: cycles chose the better method more often than complete graphs, and more slowly; density, not centrality, predicted failure. | [THEORY-146](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-146.md) | Industry can bias a scientific community toward a worse treatment without corrupting any individual, by selectively funding researchers whose methods already favour its product, provided researchers differ in method and both influence and the training of newcomers follow productivity; an independent funder counteracts this only if it discounts industry-funded work, and one that funds on productivity alone makes it worse | Holman & Bruner (2017), [LIT-744](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-744.md). | [THEORY-148](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-148.md) | A group learning by trying needs diversity in what its members pursue that lasts long enough to survive misleading early evidence and then gives way to consensus; limited communication and stubborn priors each supply it, and together they make it permanent, so the group never settles | Zollman (2010), [LIT-735](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-735.md): in a bandit model with beta priors, sparse networks and extreme priors each maintain diversity of pursuit and each improve reliability, but combined they keep diversity alive so long that agents fail to converge. | [THEORY-178](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-178.md) v3 | In an ensemble of sign-consistent Boolean rules on the 87-gene core of E. coli's regulatory network, a transient knockout or overexpression of one gene can leave the network in a different attractor after release, and every gene that does so reaches a strongly connected component containing a positive circuit | Zhao, Wytock, Reynolds and Motter (2024), [LIT-854](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-854.md). | [THEORY-188](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-188.md) v2 | In a random graph whose nodes lie in a hyperbolic disk and connect by distance, a power-law degree distribution and strong clustering follow from the geometry: the degree exponent is set by node density relative to curvature, clustering by a temperature, and removing the angular, metric part of the distance leaves the configuration model | Krioukov, Papadopoulos, Kitsak, Vahdat and Boguñá (2010), [LIT-865](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-865.md): derived, in a large-distance approximation, for a model in the hyperbolic plane, with simulations. γ = 2α/ζ + 1; clustering falls from its maximum at T = 0 to zero at a transition at T = 1; a circle model with power-law hidden degrees is the same ensemble once degree is radial depth; dropping the angular term gives the configuration model. | [THEORY-190](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-190.md) v3 | Under geometric coarse-graining of the S¹ hidden-metric network model, which merges blocks of r angular neighbours into supernodes linked if any of their members were, the supernodes' link probability approaches the S¹ form with β kept, κ′ = (Σκ^β)^{1/β}, μ′ = μ/r and R′ = R/r, its ratio to that form tending to 1 as their separation grows large against the block width and the coupling μκ′κ″; between nearby supernodes it exceeds that form | García-Pérez, Boguñá and Serrano (2017), [LIT-869](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-869.md): derived to first order, checked on one synthetic network over eight layers and on six real ones. Supernode hidden degree is the ℓ^β sum of its members'; β is invariant. The record proves the closure at large separation, with relative error of order β times the block width over the separation, and computes that between neighbouring supernodes the union of member links exceeds the S¹ form (by 32–86% in a worked example with two-node blocks). The source's flow ⟨k⟩′ = r^ν⟨k⟩, with ν = 2/(γ−1) − 1 or 2/β − 1, rests on the closure at every separation and is [QUESTION-203](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-203.md). It does not show that real networks are generated by a hidden metric space, or that the nested layers are a hierarchy found in the data. | Active |
| [THEORY-193](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-193.md) v2 | A simplicial complex grown by gluing each new d-simplex to one (d − 1)-face, by a rule that uses no geometry, has a 1-skeleton whose geodesic triangles are 2-thin at every size, so hyperbolic network geometry in Gromov's sense is an outcome of the combinatorial growth; the equal-link drawing as ideal simplices is a convention, a tiling of the hyperbolic plane for d = 2 in the manifold flavor but not a tiling of hyperbolic d-space for d ≥ 3 | Bianconi and Rahmede (2017), [LIT-867](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-867.md), read in [NOTE-678](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-678.md), for the model, the degree law and the ideal-simplex drawing. The coarse hyperbolicity of the graph is the record's: the source asserts the hyperbolic geometry through its drawing and measures nothing on the graph. Every such complex has a 1-skeleton with 2-thin geodesic triangles, whatever the flavor, so its hyperbolicity is a property of the network. The constant-curvature picture, ideal simplices in the Poincaré ball, is a choice of drawing. It tiles H² for d = 2 in the manifold flavor, and for d ≥ 3 it is not a tiling. This says nothing about whether real networks grow this way. | Active |
| [THEORY-242](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-242.md) v2 | A spiral of silence can make a small, fixed minority opinion look far more widespread than it is without any member changing belief, and in the model that shows it the network's direct distortion of what members see is small | Vilone and Polizzi (2024), [LIT-939](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-939.md), read in full in [NOTE-810](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-810.md). | [THEORY-254](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-254.md) | Tangle-defined cohesion matches network communities only where community structure is strongly delineated, and tangles of one to three vertices recur beside the ones that do | Salter-Duke (2024), [LIT-955](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-955.md), a PhD thesis read in full in [NOTE-814](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-814.md). Edge-connectivity tangles, computed exactly at low order on eleven small real networks, give communities close to standard methods where structure is strong (yeast PPI) and none or almost none where it is weak (karate club, C. elegans, college football at the orders reached), and where tangles divide a network some hold only one to three vertices. The relation is read by eye from eight networks, and the vertex sets depend on the author's assignment rule. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-276](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-276.md) v2 | In a network of identical units with identical couplings, the orbits of the graph's symmetry group are synchronization clusters, and a cluster moved only by its own factor of the group can lose synchrony while the others keep it | Pecora et al. (2014), [LIT-960](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-960.md), read in [NOTE-775](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-775.md): eq. (1), the IRR block-diagonalization (eqs. 2–4, 7), the derivation of isolated desynchronization (eq. 6) and an 11-node electro-optic experiment. The pattern of clusters that can synchronize is read from the wiring; whether each does is set by the dynamics through its own transverse block. Symmetry is sufficient, not necessary, for clusters. | [THEORY-321](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-321.md) v4 | Under repeated DeGroot averaging in a strongly connected society, the consensus converges to the truth as the society grows if and only if the largest influence weight vanishes, so network structure alone, not the members' common updating rule, decides whether the group belief is right | Golub & Jackson (2010), [LIT-999](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-999.md), Proposition 2 with Lemma 1, Corollary 1, Proposition 3 and Theorem 1, read in [NOTE-840](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-840.md) with the main proofs checked. | [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md) v3 | In one study of a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data, each element's top layer drawn geometrically, greedy search on uniform random data in 8 dimensions needed a number of distance computations that grew no worse than logarithmically with the number of items and stayed below a single-layer navigable graph's at every size tested, and in 4 dimensions the beam width needed for a fixed recall saturated; the logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded degree, which the index does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the measured growth departs from it | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) from arXiv v4. | [THEORY-370](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-370.md) | On an n × n lattice whose nodes also get long-range links drawn with probability proportional to lattice distance to the power −r, a searcher that knows only the target's position and the links of nodes already reached delivers in expected time polylogarithmic in n only at r = 2: greedy routing then takes O((log n)²) steps, while for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such searcher needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) steps and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))), even at r = 0 where short paths exist | Kleinberg (2000), [LIT-1103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1103.md), read in [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md). Proved for the two-dimensional lattice: with nodes, local links and the number of long-range links fixed, changing only the exponent r of the long-range link distribution moves the expected delivery time of the best decentralized searcher from O((log n)²) at r = 2 to a power of n at every other r, including r = 0, where paths of polylogarithmic length exist. The upper bound is proved only for one local and one long-range link per node; the k-dimensional statement (r = k) is asserted, not proved; the family is inverse power laws of a distance every node can compute, so it does not show that no other link structure is navigable. | Active |
| [THEORY-385](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-385.md) v2 | In HNSW over 10-dimensional data in 100 isolated clusters, linking each new item to its nearest neighbours leaves part of the bottom layer unreachable from the entry point and caps recall well short of 1 however wide the query search, while linking a candidate only when it is nearer the new item than to any neighbour already kept keeps that layer connected and reaches recall near 1 with about half the links; on uniform data at 10 and 64 dimensions the two rules differ little; shown in Malkov and Yashunin's own tests on 10 million points and in an independent re-run on 30,000, which found the nearest-neighbour rule capped at a recall@10 of 0.72 to 0.83 against 0.999, at matched build cost too | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md). In HNSW, each new element's neighbours are chosen either as its M nearest candidates or by a pruning rule that keeps a candidate only if it is nearer the new element than to any neighbour already kept, a rule related to the relative neighbourhood graph. On 10M random d = 10 vectors in 100 isolated clusters, nearest-neighbour links failed to reach high recall and the pruning rule did not. In every test reported, the rule was at least as good. Its gain was largest at low dimension, at high recall, and on clustered data, and small on uniform or very high-dimensional data. These are the authors' benchmarks: one clustered dataset, synthetic, with no independent replication in this reading. Re-run independently at smaller scale on promotion (2026-10-20), with the same result. | Active |
| [THEORY-421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-421.md) v2 | In HGCN embeddings of two synthetic 3-ary trees trained for link prediction or node classification, distance from the origin is only a partial reading of hierarchical level: the root is not innermost (distance 1.8–3.3 against a minimum of 1.2–2.4) and level order is recovered for 69–75% of node pairs; a loss built only on pairwise distances leaves the origin arbitrary | Yang, Zhou, Ying, Chen & King (2023), [LIT-871](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-871.md), read in [NOTE-669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-669.md). | [THEORY-422](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-422.md) | In the standard formal models of group learning, no communication network is best for every epistemic problem: costly transmission favours minimally connected or star networks, pooling of estimates by averaging favours regular networks, and learning by trying in bandit problems can favour sparse ones, so a group's network cannot be judged until its learning problem is known | Zollman (2013), [LIT-716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-716.md), a survey read in [NOTE-567](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-567.md). Each result it gathers is proved or simulated in its source (Bala and Goyal, Jackson and Wolinsky, DeGroot, Hegselmann and Krause, Zollman). Under their idealisations the optimal structure changes with the problem, so neither "too little communication" nor unequal centrality is by itself an epistemic pathology. It is a claim about models: utilitarian optimality only, with fairness, robustness and the route to the optimum left out. | Active |
| [THEORY-456](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-456.md) | Iterating Ollivier–Ricci flow on edge weights lengthens edges between communities relative to edges within them, so a weight threshold can separate the communities; but the separation is proved only on symmetric clique graphs under the uniform neighbour measure, and there only by a constant factor for gateway edges, and on a two-block stochastic block model the method fails at an inter/intra ratio near 0.55, where other methods still recover the blocks and well short of the detectability threshold near 0.78 | Ni, Lin, Luo & Gao (2019), [LIT-004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-004.md), read in full with its SI in [NOTE-006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-006.md), which checked Lemma E.1 by linear programming and iterated the proof's matrix. [THEORY-178](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-178.md) is the model result this rests on. No such perturbation has been done in cells ([QUESTION-172](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-172.md)). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-799](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-799.md) | Under geometric coarse-graining of the S¹ hidden-metric network model the average degree flows as r^ν, with ν = 2/(γ − 1) − 1 when the degree exponent γ sets it and 2/β − 1 when β does, so the coarse-grained networks run toward a complete graph for γ < 3 or β < 2 and toward a ring otherwise | The degree flow that [THEORY-190](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-190.md)'s title carried before the promotion audit (batch 048) narrowed it to the asymptotic closure of the S¹ connection law. García-Pérez, Boguñá and Serrano (2017), [LIT-869](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-869.md), derive it to first order by treating the coarse-grained graph as an S¹ model at every separation. The record's exact computation shows that treatment fails between nearby supernodes, so the flow is unproved. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-803](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-803.md) | Real complex networks embedded in the hyperbolic plane are self-similar under geometric renormalization, their coarse-grained layers keeping the degree distribution, clustering and degree–degree correlations of the original, and this self-similarity is evidence that a hidden metric space underlies them | The empirical claim [THEORY-190](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-190.md) set aside when the promotion audit (batch 048) narrowed it to the model. García-Pérez, Boguñá and Serrano (2017), [LIT-869](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-869.md), find six embedded real networks self-similar under the renormalization and call this new evidence of hidden metric spaces. The collapse was judged by eye over two to five layers with no null ordering of the circle. Filed under [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-815](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-815.md) | Layering a navigable small-world graph on nested random subsets of the data, with links separated by length scale and each layer's degree capped, makes greedy nearest-neighbour search cost grow logarithmically with the number of items on data of low intrinsic dimension, where the single-layer graph's cost grows polylogarithmically | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md), argue that HNSW's hierarchy is what makes greedy search logarithmic: constant cost per layer over O(log N) layers, against the polylogarithmic cost of their earlier flat graph. The record holds as measured, in [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md), logarithmic-or-better cost on uniform data in 8 dimensions and a saturating beam width in 4. The bound is derived only for exact Delaunay layers, which HNSW does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the paper's own scaling departs from a logarithm, so the thesis is stated for low intrinsic dimension. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-825](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-825.md) | Hyperbolic graph embedding models trained on task losses that never mention the hierarchy do not place a tree's root nearest the origin, and their distance from the origin orders hierarchical levels only partly | Yang, Zhou, Ying, Chen & King (2023), [LIT-871](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-871.md), read in [NOTE-669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-669.md), assert for hyperbolic graph models in general what they measured for HGCN on two synthetic trees: the root is not innermost and radius reads level only partly. The general form was the lead clause of [THEORY-421](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-421.md) until that account was narrowed to the measurement on 2026-10-20 ([ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v4); it is filed here so that it stays a thesis evidence can confirm or reject. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-845](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-845.md) | In Weatherall, O'Connor and Bruner's network model a policy maker's credence depends on the evidence it has received only through the total excess of successes over failures of the new action, so a propagandist's effect is the excess of failures it adds; for the same pulls, running single-trial studies and publishing the failures adds at least as large an excess as any other division into studies, which is why biased production does best with the smallest studies | Weatherall, O'Connor and Bruner (2020; arXiv 2018), [LIT-1341](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1341.md), read in [NOTE-1038](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1038.md). With two symmetric hypotheses, each result's likelihood ratio depends only on successes minus failures, so the audience's belief is a monotone function of the cumulative excess; whoever chooses what the audience sees chooses that number. It holds for the paper's two-point hypothesis space and naive updating, and says nothing about richer hypothesis spaces or audiences that model the selection. | Active |
| [THEORY-855](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-855.md) | In Bala–Goyal network models of unbiased scientists testing a slightly better new action, a propagandist who forwards to Bayesian policy makers only those real results that favour the worse action can leave the policy makers near-certain of the false theory while the scientists converge on the true one; the effect weakens as the policy makers hear more scientists, as the better action's advantage grows and as each study gets larger | Weatherall, O'Connor and Bruner (2020; arXiv 2018), [LIT-1341](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1341.md), read in [NOTE-1038](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1038.md). No result is fabricated and no scientist is biased; the audience is misled because it updates on a selected sample as if it were not selected. It is a property of a stylized model, which the authors call "how-potentially"; it does not show that any real audience was misled this way, nor that an audience aware of the selection would be. | Active |
| [THEORY-887](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-887.md) | When an attribute is concentrated on well-connected nodes, many nodes can see it in a majority of their neighbours though it is globally rare, and the share that do grows with the correlation between degree and attribute, as the network becomes more disassortative and as its degree distribution becomes heavier-tailed | Lerman, Yan & Wu (2016), [LIT-1390](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1390.md), read in full in [NOTE-1085](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1085.md) from the PLOS ONE version. The "majority illusion": with 5% of nodes active, 60–80% of nodes in a heavy-tailed synthetic network can see an active majority among their neighbours; in disassortative real topologies, 60–70% with 20% active. A binomial model from the joint degree distribution predicts the share. The edge: the attributes are assigned by the authors on every network, real ones included, so this shows what topology permits, and nothing about what people perceive, believe or do. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-902](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-902.md) | In 30 four-person student groups discussing 15 choice dilemmas, a member's self-reported closure to influence on the next issue rose with their influence over prior outcomes, increasingly so along the sequence, and the groups' influence networks thinned and their discussions shortened while the rate of consensus did not change: evidence for a reflected-appraisal step by which influence concentrates in deliberating groups | Friedkin, Jia & Bullo (2016), [LIT-1482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1482.md), read in full from the CC BY version of record and its supplement in [NOTE-1126](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1126.md). Friedkin–Johnsen dynamics on each issue, not DeGroot. Closure and centrality both come from members' post-discussion chip allocations, and prior closure is not controlled. Supports the individual step and some structural trends; the predicted end state, one closed member and consensus on that member's view, was not reached. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-916](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-916.md) | In the DeGroot–Friedkin model, where a group reaches DeGroot consensus on each issue and each member's self-weight on the next issue equals their control over the last, with fixed relative interpersonal weights, self-weights converge from every non-autocratic start to one equilibrium ordered by the eigenvector centralities of those weights: power accumulates above a centrality threshold, is autocratic exactly when the network is a star and democratic exactly when it is doubly stochastic, and members whom no path of influence reaches end with none | Jia, MirTabatabaei, Friedkin & Bullo (2015), [LIT-1146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1146.md), read in [NOTE-1135](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1135.md) from the version of record posted on the author's site; proofs skimmed. Theorems about a model, not findings about groups. The empirical companion, [LIT-1482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1482.md) ([THEORY-902](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-902.md)), uses anchored dynamics and a changing network, whose attractor is autocracy rather than this interior equilibrium. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-960](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-960.md) | In DeGroot's model, where each member repeatedly replaces its opinion by a fixed weighted average of all members' current opinions, F⁽ⁿ⁾ = PⁿF, the group reaches a consensus from every starting set of opinions exactly when the chain P has a single closed class of communicating members and that class is aperiodic; the consensus is then Σπᵢ Fᵢ with π the unique stationary vector, πP = π, which gives members outside the closed class no weight; two closed classes, or one periodic class, give no consensus | DeGroot (1974), [LIT-1527](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1527.md), read in [NOTE-1157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1157.md). Repeated averaging with fixed weights is a Markov chain run on opinions, and whether it ends in agreement is a question about the chain's closed classes and their periods. It is not about how much each member trusts itself. The weights are fixed and no evidence enters, so nothing here says the consensus is right, and the periodic failure is a discrete-time one. | Active |
| [THEORY-993](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-993.md) | In the mixed membership stochastic blockmodel the probability of an edge from p to q, given the memberships, is (1 − ρ)π_pᵀBπ_q, so the graph's likelihood given the memberships is unchanged by π ↦ Rπ, B ↦ R⁻ᵀBR⁻¹ for any invertible R that keeps the memberships on the simplex and B in [0, 1], a continuum around any solution with B's rates strictly between 0 and 1; and the sparsity parameter ρ enters only through (1 − ρ)B, so it is fixed by nothing but the bound B ≤ 1, and the paper's printed estimator of it is the fraction of absent edges whatever the fit | Airoldi, Blei, Fienberg and Xing (2008), [LIT-1553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1553.md), read in [NOTE-1179](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1179.md). The paper says the blockmodel and the memberships do not compete, because one is global and asymmetric and the other local and symmetric. Given the memberships they do: a change of block basis moves every node's memberships toward the centre and sharpens B, with the same edge probabilities. What can still separate them is the Dirichlet family assumed for memberships, not the graph. The confounding of ρ with B's scale is exact even in the marginal likelihood. | Active |
| [THEORY-1008](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1008.md) | Mixed memberships fitted by a fifteen-block MMSB to 871 yeast proteins' curated physical interactions carry information about the proteins' top-level MIPS functions beyond what the functions' base rates give: after mapping blocks to functions on 87 proteins, thresholded memberships predicted the other proteins' annotations with about 87% accuracy, against about 70% for random guessing at the right proportions | Airoldi, Blei, Fienberg and Xing (2008), [LIT-1553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1553.md), §4.3.2 and Figs. 10–12, read in [NOTE-1179](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1179.md). The batch's one check of inferred mixed memberships against labels the model never saw. The reported margin is over a weak baseline, so it shows less than it seems: probably some information, not yet how much. It says nothing about whether the fifteen blocks are the fifteen functions. | Proposed |
